summary: A 0.1–0.4 m rosette tolerates nickel released by weathering iron-nickel impact debris. It concentrates nickel in protected cellular compartments and carries violet-red, alkaloid-defended foliage. Its patch distribution helps trace the bent ejecta ray; neither colour nor absence proves a shard's position or reveals the second capsule's purpose (F22, F25, F26).

links: Weathering impact debris creates locally nickel-rich soil patches.
Selective transport and binding limit damage to sensitive cellular machinery.
Sequestration isolates accumulated nickel in storage compartments.
The herb persists where less tolerant competitors struggle.
chains.play: Compare plant patches with exposed fragments and follow a sequence of suitable sites along the bent ejecta ray.
chains.weakness: Tolerance has limits; excessive contamination, drought or unsuitable substrate excludes the plant, leaving gaps in the botanical trail.
observe: Dense rosettes cluster around some weathered fragments while nearby ordinary soil supports other vegetation.
Follow several patches to reveal a bend rather than a straight radial line.
Inspect an eroded patch edge to find mineral-stained debris beneath ordinary soft roots.

plausibility.summary: Nickel accumulation is biologically credible; metallic leaves, iron-powered metabolism and automatic soil purification are excluded. The 12,000-year-old crater supports a vegetation mosaic, and five shards need not each have a plant marker.

analogues.mechanism: Metal transport, ligand binding and compartmentation permit exceptional tissue nickel loads. Transfer to meteoritic soil is an ecological extrapolation. [Krämer](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-arplant-042809-112156)

links: Open patches expose leaves to strong light while herbivores encounter low foliage.
Protective pigments overlay green photosynthetic tissue.
Persistent red-violet veins accompany alkaloid defence.
Colour warns against eating; patch location provides the separate geological clue.
chains.play: Learn to separate a poison warning from a habitat clue and avoid offering the leaves as food.
chains.weakness: Purple foliage is not a nickel assay; exposed leaves can become darker without a corresponding increase in soil metal.
observe: Shaded leaves retain red-violet veins against a greener blade.
Exposed leaves carry a broader violet overlay.
Equally purple plants occur at different distances from visible impact fragments.

plausibility.summary: The pigment analogue supports photoprotection, while the honest alkaloid warning follows F25. Colour alone does not quantify nickel, and the crater receives no invented elevation or high-altitude UV value.

analogues.mechanism: Foliar anthocyanins provide an analogue for photoprotection and stress-associated colour; reliable alkaloid signalling is a planet-canon property. [Gould](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1082902/)

poison.signal: Persistent red-violet veins warn of alkaloids; accumulated nickel adds a separate hazard that colour does not quantify.

gameplay.cover: Low rosettes obscure small ground objects but cannot conceal a standing creature.
gameplay.notes: Use the plant as an imperfect substrate indicator. Player-lineage alkaloid detoxification does not establish nickel tolerance. Shared biochemistry does not remove chemical toxicity, and babosa's mineral diet does not establish safe nickel accumulation.

relations.note: Learns the association between patch distribution and weathered impact debris while avoiding ingestion.
The red-veined leaves fall within their established dietary avoidance; open patches also offer little sun shelter.
May border pioneer crusts on exposed crater rock where moisture and chemistry permit both.

generator.trunk: None; short perennial root crown with ordinary flexible roots in weathered soil.

leaf.type: Waxy spoon-shaped blade with visible veins

overlay_rules: Persistent red-violet veins accompany alkaloid defence.
Exposed blades develop broader violet-red screening.
Do not encode nickel concentration as metallic sheen or a fixed purple intensity.

placement.slope: Stable crater-floor pockets and suitable deposits along the single bent ejecta ray
placement.wetness: Seasonally moist, freely draining soil; growth slows during drought
placement.soil: Weathered tuff locally enriched by iron-nickel debris; exclude both ordinary soils and lethal contamination extremes
placement.density: Discontinuous substrate-controlled patches; apply the crater-and-ejecta mask before broad island bounds, since crater elevation is unspecified

generator.seasonal: Perennial crowns produce fresh leaves after rain and reduce exposed foliage during drought; winter response follows the crater's actual placement.
generator.wind_response: Low flexible leaves bend close to the ground; eroding sediment can expose or bury the root crown.

journal.en: Violet leaves, scattered metal. Follow where it grows, not how brightly it shines.
journal.es: Hojas violetas, metal disperso. Sigue dónde crece, no cuánto brilla.

changelog.what: flora pass: 7 voices drafted and peer-reviewed, Composer botanical referee, sol chaired and applied the fixes

observe: Map several patches before inferring the ejecta ray's direction.
Compare violet intensity with shade, then compare patch location with weathered debris.
Inspect gaps in the trail for erosion or unsuitable soil rather than assuming a missing shard.
secrets: Several patches together reveal the ejecta ray's bend, helping narrow the search for the five shards.
A dense patch may surround buried weathering debris without marking an intact shard.
Its ecology provides no answer to what the second capsule did.
